source.title: Emergent Abilities in Reduced-Scale Generative Language Models
source.authors: Sherin Muckatira; Vijeta Deshpande; V. Lialin; Anna Rumshisky

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some equations in the extracted Figure 2 are garbled, so their coefficients and exponents cannot be read reliably.
record.tranche_reason: Fits power curves to held-out pretraining loss against compute, data size and model size, using a different data and model scale setup from the original scaling-law studies; also evaluates downstream performance across model configurations.
record.gate_note: Figure 2 reports curve fits over 25 compute-optimal instances and R² values, but its displayed equation coefficients and exponents are garbled in the supplied text. Table 7 reports held-out perplexities. Table 2 reports zero-shot task averages. Figure 4 reports an accuracy trend. Few-shot results in Table 3 concern changes with the number of examples, rather than the scaling variables named by the claim, and are not included as claim-version rows.
record.test_reason: Section 5.3 fits L = A·x^B to held-out pretraining loss against FLOPs, data size and model size for small models trained on vocabulary-simplified text. This is a new data setting with a direct result on V1. The study also evaluates zero-shot accuracy across model sizes (Table 2, Figure 4, Table 8), which bears on V6. Its main aim is emergent zero-shot ability, but the power-law result is its own.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The headline conclusion is that small models pretrained on vocabulary-simplified data show enhanced zero-shot ability on filtered tasks. For example, Simple 165M averages 0.64 on filtered data, above Pythia 1B's 0.61 on standard data. These models also follow power laws in loss versus FLOPs, data and model size (R2 0.86/0.80/0.75). Few-shot gains did not appear at these sizes.
record.recipe_differences: Uses power-curve fitting, but tests small models trained on vocabulary-filtered simplified data; it uses a FLOPs formula that includes embedding parameters, unlike the cited Kaplan calculation. It does not reproduce the original broad-scale training setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Evaluation distribution affects downstream averages; Figure 4 examines hidden size and layer count, but the text does not report quantified effects beyond the plotted trends.

fits_no_version.finding: Within the tested range, loss falls faster per unit change in model size than in data size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Relative loss sensitivity to N vs D in small-model, simplified-data regimes

record.problems: The loss-law fits are reported on 25 compute-optimal instances from a small, simplified-data setup. The extracted Figure 2 equations are garbled, and no uncertainty intervals or out-of-range prediction test are reported. The authors note that vocabulary filtering changes sequence-length and word-frequency distributions and that results should be understood within the properties of that pretraining data.
record.rows_left_out: The additional Table 7 parameter configurations (other than the 8-layer size sweep recorded here) and regular-model perplexity on the simple held-out set are not separately extracted. Detailed task-by-task zero-shot scores in Table 2 and the per-configuration scores in Appendix Tables 8–10 are not included; the Table 2 aggregate averages are recorded. These tables report many additional model-condition-task results, so the record prioritizes scaling-law fits and the aggregate downstream comparisons under the 60-row cap.

untested.parts: Several orders of magnitude: params span only about 1M–165M, with 2.1B tokens at most for the fits. Fitted exponents are unreadable, so they cannot be compared with Kaplan/Chinchilla.
No forecast of larger runs from small-run fits.
No compute-optimal N/D allocation versus compute is reported.
Depth and width vary, but never at a fixed parameter count.
No other modality, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer scaling.
No fitted mapping from scale or loss to downstream accuracy; there are only monotonic trends.
Uses an embedding-inclusive FLOPs formula but does not compare fitting choices.

missing.what: Fitted A and B coefficients for the three power laws; the extracted text is garbled and they are needed to compare exponents with Kaplan/Chinchilla
Table 8 per-configuration PIQA/ARC-Easy accuracies, e.g. simple PIQA filtered 0.526 (h32) to 0.653 (h1024, 8 layers); quantifies the Fig 4 trend

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 limits_scope label (Simple 165M filtered vs standard) compared evaluation distributions, not scale, so it does not bear on V6. It is replaced by a within-family size comparison. The Table 2 Pythia/OPT scores are the authors' own evaluations, so they are kept as rows. The t7 sweeps use a fixed token count, so they are not compute-optimal and data may bottleneck the larger models.

versions.untested_parts: The loss fits are on the simplified-language setting and the tested small-model/data range; the paper does not establish the claim over several orders of magnitude or test all other setups.
No out-of-range prediction test comparing forecasts from small runs with much larger runs is reported.
The study fits loss against compute, data size and model size, but does not report how the loss-minimising parameter and token allocation changes with compute.
Although configurations vary in hidden size and number of layers, the study does not isolate architecture effects at a fixed parameter count.
No other modality, repeated-data regime, fine-tuning or transfer scaling law is tested.
The study reports zero-shot performance and an accuracy trend for selected tasks, but does not establish a general quantitative mapping from pretraining loss to downstream performance.
The study notes a different FLOPs-counting formula from Kaplan et al., but does not vary fitting choices to test their effect on exponents or allocation trends.

relationships.condition: Small LLaMA-style models (about 1M–165M) trained on vocabulary-simplified SlimPajama, 25 compute-optimal points
relationships.reason: Power fits give R2 0.86 (FLOPs), 0.80 (data) and 0.75 (params). Held-out perplexity falls monotonically with size for both simple and regular data (FLOPs-fit, data-fit, model-fit, t7 rows).
relationships.display_finding: Power-law fits achieved R² of 0.86 for compute, 0.80 for data and 0.75 for parameters, while held-out perplexity decreased with size on simplified and regular data.

relationships.condition: Pythia and OPT families (125M–1.3B) zero-shot averages; own models' PIQA/ARC-Easy capacity sweeps
relationships.reason: Averages rise with size within each family, e.g. OPT 0.58→0.60→0.66 and Pythia 0.57→0.58→0.61. The paper states accuracy improves with capacity (Fig 4).
relationships.display_finding: Average scores increased with size from 0.58 to 0.60 to 0.66 for OPT and 0.57 to 0.58 to 0.61 for Pythia, alongside reported capacity gains on PIQA and ARC-Easy.

relationships.condition: Simple models (100M vs 165M, 22B tokens) on standard, unfiltered tasks
relationships.reason: Average zero-shot accuracy is 0.56 at both sizes, so there is no gain with scale under distribution shift (t2-simple165-std vs t2-simple100-std).
relationships.display_finding: Average zero-shot accuracy remained 0.56 at both sizes under distribution shift.
